source.title: Parts-of-Speech as Emergent Categories in SAE Latent Space
source.authors: Alessandro Bondielli; Lucia C. Passaro; Serena Auriemma; Alessandro Lenci

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how POS information is organized in an LLM's SAE latents and finds groups of multiple latents, category overlap, and lexical/contextual contributions. This refines the claim that SAE latents are atomic, canonical units, but it does not test toy-model superposition or capacity competition.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports probe comparisons, controls, and layer analyses. Values used only to select a layer or parameters are not recorded as separate findings. Cited results from prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study uses its own measurements of LLaMA-3-8B SAE latents to argue that POS categories are carried by overlapping groups of latents, not atomic units. This bears on V4, whether a dictionary recovers sparse, localized features in an LLM, and qualifies V5, whether SAE latents are canonical units. It does not test toy models, capacity competition, causes of polysemanticity or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that POS is recoverable from SAE activations and carried by compact but distributed, category-dependent groups of latents, not atomic grammatical features. The groups are stable on held-out data and largely additive on controlled examples, but only partly category-specific. They also partly track lexical, positional and annotation regularities. The compactness gradient reflects lexical variability rather than abstraction.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes POS recoverability and organization in a pretrained LLM's SAE activations, using probes, salience, coverage, and held-out evaluation; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports layer-dependent variation, including redistribution of which latents a POS uses, while aggregate group size and performance remain broadly similar across Layers 2, 15, and 30. It also reports variation across POS categories and controlled templates.

fits_no_version.finding: The compactness of a POS's latent group tracks the lexical variability of its word forms. Closed classes are covered by small groups that can be form-specific; the authors say this is not graded abstraction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How compact the SAE latent group for a linguistic category is reflects how varied its word forms are, not how abstract the category is.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study uses one base model and one SAE, and its localization relies on linear probe coefficients rather than causal interventions. The controlled dataset is small and restricted mainly to noun and verb constructions. The paper notes that lexical identity, surface form, position, and context contribute to some activations. The text gives inconsistent real-probe macro-F1 values: Section 5.4 states 0.97 while Table 2 reports 0.78.
record.rows_left_out: The per-POS rows of Table 7 are not separately extracted; the aggregate accuracy and macro-average results are recorded in r7. Figure-only per-category probe and layer plots are summarized where the text provides an explicit description, rather than transcribing every plotted value.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity sweep, phase transition or geometry.
No capacity competition or importance-based dedicated dimensions.
No mechanisms of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
Only one model, one SAE and one concept family (POS). There is no causal evidence that the model uses these latents, and no measure of how features spread over neurons.
Completeness, and stability across SAE seeds or sizes, are not tested. Canonicity is examined only for POS categories.
Dimensionality of features is not tested.

missing.what: Per-category distinctiveness D(c), ranging 0.093 (INTJ) to 0.350 (ADP/DET), with 27% of X tokens activating none of the group's latents. Shows that category specificity varies by tag.
Distinctiveness across layers: 0.15±0.03 (L2), 0.32±0.09 (L15), 0.27±0.07 (L30). Category specificity depends on the layer.
Single latents recur as top coefficients across several closed-class POS (e.g. latent 72975 in AUX/CCONJ/PART), which the authors call possibly polyfunctional latents.
Per-template variation on controlled data: recall falls to 0.80 for 'There is' noun templates vs about 0.97 for the others.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. Probe coefficients are not causal evidence, as the authors acknowledge. The text gives the real probe's macro F1 inconsistently (0.97 in Sec. 5.4 vs 0.78 in Table 2). Rows r13–r16 and r17–r19 partly duplicate r6/r7 at layer 30.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature sparsity sweep, feature importance sweep, or superposition geometry are tested.
The study does not test capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or causes of polysemantic neurons.
The study does not investigate mechanisms that produce polysemantic neurons independently of capacity pressure.
Tests POS-related recoverability and localization with one LLM and one SAE; does not measure general feature distribution across LLMs or establish causal use.
Tests selected POS-related latent groups for compactness, held-out activity, and overlap. Does not test whether SAE features are complete or canonical for all model representations or other concepts.
Does not test whether the underlying features are one-dimensional directions versus multidimensional features; multiple latents per POS category do not resolve that question.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: One-vs-rest L1-regularized logistic regression probes on SAE activations
rows.value: High F1 for most categories; closed-class and low-variability labels are easier to recover, while lexically heterogeneous or less frequent categories score lower. Exact per-category values are shown in Figure 2.
rows.note: The text describes POS distinctions as consistently recoverable; exact plotted values are not stated in the text.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Counted positively weighted latents in one-vs-rest POS probes
rows.value: Each POS distinction is supported by multiple positively contributing latents, not a single-latent representation.
rows.note: The authors describe the organization as distributed but non-uniform.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Counted non-zero probe coefficients by POS group
rows.measure: Mean ± standard deviation of non-zero latents
rows.note: Open-class probes had the highest mean number of non-zero coefficients.
rows.check: These are counts of non-zero L1 probe coefficients, which depend on the regularization C. They describe the probe rather than whether latents are units. States across r3–r5 were also inconsistent (observed vs partial) for the same kind of count. Not V4 evidence by itself.

rows.operation_detail: Counted non-zero probe coefficients by POS group

rows.note: Closed-class probes used fewer non-zero coefficients on average than open-class probes.
rows.check: Same as r3: a descriptive coefficient count, with no expected effect that could be partial.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: United the per-category minimal latent groups reaching 95% coverage
rows.measure: Size of selected latent union and proportion shared across 2+ POS
rows.value: 498 latents; 12% shared between 2+ POS
rows.note: The selected set is compact relative to the attested SAE latent space, but some selected latents are shared across categories.

source_check.correct: V4: observed. The selected union contains 498 latents, with 12% shared across multiple POS categories. Sharing does not establish incomplete recovery under V4 or test canonicality under V5; remove the V5 link.
source_check.problem: The partial state conflates overlapping POS associations with incomplete V4 recovery and a test of V5.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE

rows.value: Compact-set classifier performance described as comparable to the full SAE representation; Table 7 reports accuracy 0.89 and macro-average F1 0.81
rows.note: The paper reports that the selected set preserves most information needed for multiclass POS discrimination.

source_check.correct: Observed for V4; cannot_determine for V5, whose link should be removed. Compact-set classification tests information recoverability, not completeness, stability or canonicality of SAE units.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2; Figures 5 and 12; Appendix B.2, Table 7.

rows.value: Most values are ≥ 0.95
rows.note: The paper states that the selected groups remain active on unseen tokens from their target categories.
rows.check: Held-out recall of selected groups shows stability across data splits. It is not the stability V5 means (across SAE training runs or dictionary sizes), so the V5 link is removed.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Applied selected latent groups as pseudo-multilabel POS indicators
rows.value: Precision 0.192; recall 0.937; F1 0.318
rows.note: The paper describes precision as limited and recall as very high, with variation across templates.

source_check.correct: Controlled-template averages: precision 0.192, recall 0.937, F1 0.318. These show partial category specificity of group-activation indicators. V4 recoverability is observed elsewhere; this indicator does not determine completeness or canonicality under V5.
source_check.problem: Partial indicator specificity is treated as a partial effect for claim versions that do not require one-to-one POS detectors.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Assigned random UPOS labels by word type and reran the probe
rows.baseline: Real-label probe: 0.88 accuracy / 0.97 macro F1, as stated in Section 5.4
rows.value: 0.54 accuracy / 0.42 macro F1
rows.note: The authors say the gap supports POS recoverability not being simply reducible to lexical memorization. These real-label figures differ from Table 2's reported macro F1.
rows.check: This is a control. The real-label baseline macro F1 of 0.97 in Sec. 5.4 conflicts with 0.78 in Table 2. The real probe clearly exceeds the random word-type control, so the state is observed, not partial.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compared POS probes using SAE activations, layer 30 residual activations, and layer 0 embeddings

conditions.value: SAE uses approximately 8 times fewer features

rows.baseline: Layer 30: accuracy 0.92, macro F1 0.84; Layer 0: accuracy 0.88, macro F1 0.78
rows.value: SAE: accuracy 0.88, macro F1 0.78
rows.note: The authors do not claim SAE probing superiority; they emphasize localization.
rows.check: A baseline comparison. The dense layer-30 probe beats the SAE probe (0.92/0.84 vs 0.88/0.78), and the SAE only equals layer-0 embeddings. So the SAE recovers POS but adds no recoverability over dense activations.

source_check.correct: V4: observed. SAE accuracy/macro F1 are 0.88/0.78, versus 0.92/0.84 for layer-30 activations and 0.88/0.78 for embeddings. V4 does not require SAE superiority over dense probes.
source_check.problem: Lower performance than a dense probe does not make the stated V4 effect partial.

rows.check: The 0% overlap condition is the random-feature control, not an independent finding. Its role should be control. It shows the selected latents matter because performance collapses without them (0.24/0.16).

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Examined activation patterns as controlled sentences gained tokens

conditions.value: Noun and verb constructions with added adjective/adverb and punctuation

rows.measure: Qualitative additivity and category-related activation changes
rows.value: Adding a word generally activates additional latents associated with its POS; e.g., adding loyal to There is a dog activates more ADJ-associated latents. Related-category latents can already be active before the corresponding word is added.
rows.note: The authors describe the activations as largely additive, but not category-exclusive.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compared POS-group activation distributions across controlled template variants
rows.value: A slight shift in the activation distribution when an adjective is added
rows.note: The paper links the shift to cross-category co-activation.
rows.check: A qualitative 'slight shift' in a KDE, with no number. It cannot show whether latents are canonical units, and there is no V4 effect.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compared POS-group activation distributions across controlled template variants
rows.value: Only a minor shift across sentence types
rows.note: The authors interpret this as lower sensitivity of verb-associated latents to surrounding context than noun-associated latents.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B with EleutherAI/sae-llama-3-8b-32x SAE
rows.operation_detail: Prepended a number and punctuation to controlled templates and compared activations
rows.measure: Location of latents previously active on the initial PRON
rows.baseline: Original sentence with initial token I
rows.value: Latents firing on PRON in the original sentence shifted to the newly prepended NUM token; the paper says all tested cases showed the same behavior.
rows.note: This is evidence that some selected activations depend on position or token context, rather than being category-exclusive.
rows.check: Latents selected for PRON actually track first-token position. This shows that some selected latents encode position rather than category. The V4 link is removed.

relationships.reason: POS information is recoverable (r1) and localized in a compact set of about 500 of 130k latents (r6). That set keeps classification at 0.89 accuracy / 0.81 macro F1 (r7, r16) and fires on held-out tokens (r8). Performance falls as the set is replaced by random latents (r13–r15), it exceeds a lexical control (r11), and it is stable across layers (r17–r19).
relationships.display_finding: POS information was recoverable and localized in about 500 of 130k latents, which kept classification at 0.89 accuracy and 0.81 macro F1 and fired on held-out tokens. Performance fell as the set was replaced by random latents, it beat a lexical control, and it was stable across layers.

relationships.condition: Comparison with dense probes; controlled templates
relationships.reason: Dense layer-30 activations recover POS better than the SAE (r12). The selected groups have precision of only 0.19 on controlled data (r10), so the recovered features are not clean category detectors.
relationships.display_finding: Dense layer-30 activations recovered parts of speech better than the SAE. The selected latent groups had precision of only 0.19 on controlled data, so they are not clean category detectors.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Comparison with dense probes; controlled templates
source_check.reason: r12 shows lower probe performance than dense layer-30 activations, and r10 shows imperfect specificity of activation indicators. V4 requires neither superior probing performance nor exclusive category detectors; these conditions do not contradict its stated recoverability claim.

relationships.condition: POS categories in the layer-30 SAE latent space
relationships.reason: No POS maps to a single latent (r2). 12% of selected latents are shared across POS (r6) and mean distinctiveness is 0.27 against an exclusive value of 1 (r9). Groups fire on other categories (r10, r20), and some selected latents track first-token position rather than category (r23). SAE latents therefore do not act as atomic, canonical category units here.
relationships.display_finding: No POS mapped to a single latent: 12% of selected latents were shared across POS, mean distinctiveness was 0.27 against an exclusive value of 1, groups fired on other categories, and some latents tracked first-token position rather than category.

source_check.reason: Distributed, overlapping POS associations and positional confounds do not test whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical model units. The introduction explicitly allows linguistic categories to combine multiple underlying features; there are no dictionary-size, training-seed or completeness comparisons.
